source.title: Double Descent in Gradient Boosting Decision Trees via Split-Candidate Scaling

page_placements.theme: Tree-ensemble curve shapes depend on the capacity intervention

record.file_problem: No garbling or truncation is apparent; the supplied text includes the paper and its experimental details.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests double descent in GBDTs using split-candidate count as a single capacity axis, while refining the interpretation of earlier GBDT results that used a parameter-count axis confounded with boosting rounds and ensembling.
record.gate_note: The study directly reports test-error sweeps, kernel diagnostics, peak shifts, and training-time emergence. Results cited from other studies are not included as rows. Settings and values used only to choose the experimental protocol are not rows.
record.test_reason: The study reports its own test-RMSE sweeps showing an interior peak followed by a second descent in GBDTs (CatBoost, XGBoost, LightGBM) and kernel references. It uses a new capacity axis, the split-candidate count, with depth, rounds and ensemble size fixed. That is a new model class and setting for V4. It also tests whether a single complexity proxy (path-span crossing D_L≈n) predicts peak location across depth and sample size (V5), and whether label noise amplifies the peak (V6). It does not argue a version is wrong, so T3 fits better than the reader's T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also stress that split-candidate count is a single, consistent capacity axis, which answers the confound in earlier GBDT double-descent results. They also note that peak locations vary with sample size and dataset geometry while the pattern recurs across libraries and datasets.
record.recipe_differences: The study varies GBDT split-candidate budgets and measures RMSE, rather than scaling neural-network width or testing the original deep-network model-size, epoch, and sample-size protocols.
record.method_sensitivity: Peak location shifts with tree depth and training-set size; peak prominence rises with label-swap rate; location alignment depends on dataset geometry and the Independentized/Unique ranks transformations. The peak's visibility also depends on boosting checkpoint and CatBoost diagnostic versus default profile. Results vary by algorithm: the three GBDT libraries show peaks while the random-forest control improves monotonically.

fits_no_version.finding: Double descent in GBDTs appears on a single capacity axis (split candidates), with depth, boosting rounds and ensemble size held fixed. This answers the objection that Belkin et al.'s GBDT curve mixed rounds with ensembling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In GBDTs, double descent arises under a single consistent capacity intervention (split-candidate count), not only from parameter-count axes that conflate boosting rounds with ensembling.

record.problems: The main controlled sweeps use five resampled splits. Many curve heights and peak locations are shown only in figures rather than stated numerically. The study tests one primary dataset for controlled ablations and a finite set of tabular datasets; its path-span proxy does not closely predict transitions on original covariates in every setting.
record.rows_left_out: Per-dataset graphical curves in Figure 6 and Figures 8–9 are not separately rowed where the text reports only aggregate contrasts or mean offsets; the corresponding aggregate results are recorded in r20-r21 and r23-r30. No exact per-dataset values are stated in the text.

untested.parts: No test-error curve over boosting iterations at a fixed budget is reported in the text. Figure 5 contains such data but it is not described.
No comparison of test error across training sizes at a fixed split-candidate budget near the threshold.
Only tree ensembles and tree-kernel KGD/KRR on tabular regression are tested. No classification and no other model classes.

The epoch axis is not tested as a predictor of peak location. The measure used is the path-span proxy and kernel spectrum, not Nakkiran's EMC. The sample-size axis is tested only through the location shift along M.
Multiple or triple descent is not examined. Tuned regularization is not examined: λ is fixed at 1e-5 and the default profile uses library defaults.
No replotting against an effective parameter count. The study argues double descent arises on a single consistent axis but does not test Curth et al.'s reparameterization.

missing.what: Test RMSE over boosting iterations at a fixed M near the peak, which could show or rule out an epoch-wise fall-rise-fall.
Test RMSE compared across ntrain=500/1000/2000 at a fixed M near the peak, which would show whether more data hurts at that budget.

record.verdict_notes: Tranche changed from T5 to T3: the study demonstrates double descent in a new setting and does not dispute a version. The reader's V4 'challenges' label for the random forest (r18) is downgraded to limits_scope, because the forest's interpolation is not shown and the authors present it as evidence that boosting dynamics are needed. Most curve values appear only in figures. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: The study tests GBDTs, not model-wise double descent in deep neural networks.
It shows that a peak over split-candidate budgets emerges as boosting proceeds, but does not measure test error as a fall-rise-fall curve over training epochs.
The sample-size sweep reports shifts in the peak's split-candidate location, not whether increasing sample count raises test error near a fixed interpolation threshold.
Tests GBDTs, KRR, and a random-forest control under the reported candidate sweeps; does not test all model classes or neural networks.

Tests a path-span proxy and empirical kernel diagnostics against peak locations under split-candidate and sample-size/depth sweeps; does not test whether one measure predicts peak location over training epochs.
Tests whether added label noise makes the peak more prominent. It does not test multiple/triple descent or whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak.
The study proposes a path-feature/kernel capacity interpretation but does not show that replotting against an effective parameter count turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.
